title: CSIRO's GenCost report finds firmed renewables the cheapest new-build electricity for Australia and large-scale nuclear the most expensive
oneLiner: The national science agency's annual cost comparison puts wind and solar with storage and transmission below every other new-build option.
body: GenCost, produced each year by CSIRO with the market operator, estimates the cost of building and running each generation technology in Australian conditions. Its recent editions find renewables with firming cheaper per megawatt-hour than new coal, gas or nuclear, and put large-scale nuclear at the top of the range because of its capital cost and build time.
contextBackground: GenCost is the reference cost study used by the Australian Energy Market Operator in system planning. It has been published annually since 2018 and is revised after public consultation each year. Its nuclear figures have been the most contested part of the report since 2023, and CSIRO has responded by publishing its assumptions and a longer discussion of them.
contextDisagreement: Critics accept the report exists and says this, but argue the comparison understates integration costs for renewables and overstates nuclear costs by assuming a first-of-a-kind build. Supporters note that each year's revision has been consulted on and the ranking has not changed.

otherClaim.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation

claimItself.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
claimItself.body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.

otherClaim.title: The east-coast gas reservation scheme starting in July 2027 will materially lower domestic gas prices

claimItself.title: The east-coast gas reservation scheme starting in July 2027 will materially lower domestic gas prices
claimItself.oneLiner: Australia has decided to reserve gas for domestic buyers. The question now is whether the scheme, as designed and then softened, will do what it was announced to do.
claimItself.body: In May 2026 the federal government announced that Queensland's three LNG export ventures must reserve a share of export volumes for Australian users from July 2027, with contracts signed before 22 December 2025 exempt. In September 2026 the rule was recast around forecast domestic demand rather than a flat share of exports. The government says prices will fall; it will not say by how much.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Because export contracts signed before 22 December 2025 are exempt, the scheme reaches too little gas to move prices for years

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Western Australia requires LNG projects to reserve 15 per cent of production for the domestic market, and its gas prices have been well below the east coast's

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Mandatory reservation will deter investment in new gas supply and worsen the shortfall it is meant to fix
